question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2019, developmental psychologist Lorcan Ondrey claimed that four-year-olds who take group music classes learn new words faster than their peers do, because music training sharpens the ability to tell apart similar-sounding speech sounds.
• A team led by Renata Quillfeather at the Ashcombe Child Study Center tested 64 four-year-olds who had attended music classes for at least a year and 64 who had not.
• In a word-learning task, each child heard six made-up object names, each repeated eight times, and then picked the named object from a set of four.
• The music-class children identified an average of 4.6 of the 6 new words correctly; the other children averaged 3.1.
• In a separate task, children heard pairs of syllables such as "ba" and "pa" that differed only slightly in timing and said whether the two syllables were the same or different.
• The music-class children correctly judged 78 percent of the pairs; the other children correctly judged 77 percent.
• All testing took place in a quiet room at each child's preschool, in sessions of about 20 minutes.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Ondrey's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Ondrey's claim: the music-class children and the other children correctly judged nearly the same share of syllable pairs, 78 percent versus 77 percent.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Ondrey's observation but not his explanation: the music-class children averaged 4.6 of the 6 new words correct to the others' 3.1, yet the two groups judged nearly the same share of syllable pairs, 78 percent versus 77 percent.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Ondrey's claim: the music-class children identified an average of 4.6 of the 6 new words correctly, compared with an average of 3.1 for the other children.
answer_d: The team's findings support Ondrey's explanation but not his observation: the two groups judged nearly the same share of syllable pairs, 78 percent versus 77 percent, yet the music-class children averaged 4.6 of the 6 new words correct to the others' 3.1.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it matches each part of Ondrey's claim to the data that bears on it. Ondrey's sentence says two things: that children in music classes learn new words faster, and that this happens because music training sharpens the ability to tell apart similar-sounding speech sounds. The word-learning task bears on the first part. The music-class children identified an average of 4.6 of the 6 new words correctly, compared with 3.1 for the other children, and because every child heard each word the same number of times, this higher score shows that the music-class children learned the words more quickly, so the faster word learning Ondrey described did appear. The syllable-pair task bears on the second part, because it directly measures the ability to tell apart similar-sounding speech sounds. There the music-class children were correct on 78 percent of the pairs and the other children on 77 percent, so the music-class children showed no sharper discrimination. The team's findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of children tested and the testing setting describe the study's method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The nearly equal syllable-pair scores (78 percent versus 77 percent) do count against Ondrey's explanation, but the claim also says that music-class children learn new words faster, and the word-learning results (4.6 versus 3.1 words) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 4.6 versus 3.1 word-learning averages do fit the first part of Ondrey's claim, that music-class children learn new words faster, but Ondrey also said this happens because of sharper discrimination of similar-sounding speech sounds, and the syllable-pair results (78 percent versus 77 percent) show no such advantage. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it reverses which part of Ondrey's claim each result supports. It cites the right numbers, but the conclusion is backward. The word-learning averages (4.6 versus 3.1) show that music-class children did learn new words faster, which supports Ondrey's observation, not undermines it. The nearly equal syllable-pair scores (78 percent versus 77 percent) show no difference in discriminating similar-sounding speech sounds, which fails to support his explanation, not confirms it. This is the pattern of swapping which part of a claim the data supports and which it does not.
